Working with large datasets

Source: vignettes/articles/million_cell_crb_artifacts.Rmd
million_cell_crb_artifacts.Rmd

Choose an expression backend

CerebroNexus stores the expression matrix either inside the .crb or in a sparse HDF5 file next to it. Select the storage with expression_matrix_mode in exportFromSeurat() or convertSeuratToCerebro():

Mode Practical use Files to keep together
embedded Small datasets and simple single-file distribution .crb
h5 On-disk sparse expression, including single-gene queries and large datasets .crb and its recorded .h5 sidecar

With h5, the Viewer reads individual genes from disk without loading the complete matrix into memory. This usually reduces startup time and memory use for large datasets, although a disk read can be slower than reading a matrix that is already in memory. h5 describes the export format, not how Seurat stores the matrix: the Seurat object does not need an H5-backed matrix.

Use the benchmark guide for measured workloads and their limits. Avoid converting a large delayed or on-disk matrix into a dense matrix merely to inspect or export it.

Store the expression matrix in an H5 file

H5 export needs the Bioconductor package HDF5Array, which provides the TENx HDF5 writer and the lazy matrix reader used at runtime:

if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("BiocManager")
}
BiocManager::install("HDF5Array")

Export from Seurat

Choose the assay and layer (called slot for compatibility with older Seurat versions) exactly as you would for an embedded export. Adding expression_matrix_mode = "h5" makes CerebroNexus write the selected matrix to a sibling H5 file and store only its relative location in the .crb:

library(CerebroNexus)

seurat <- readRDS(
  system.file(
    "extdata/examples/pbmc_seurat.rds",
    package = "CerebroNexus"
  )
)

output_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "cerebro-h5-example")
dir.create(output_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
crb_output <- file.path(output_dir, "pbmc.crb")

exportFromSeurat(
  object = seurat,
  assay = "RNA",
  slot = "data",
  file = crb_output,
  experiment_name = "PBMC",
  organism = "hg",
  groups = c("sample", "seurat_clusters"),
  nUMI = "nCount_RNA",
  nGene = "nFeature_RNA",
  expression_matrix_mode = "h5",
  verbose = TRUE
)

The exporter writes two files with the same stem, pbmc.crb and pbmc.h5. The .crb records the H5 filename in its expression-backend descriptor:

h5_output <- file.path(output_dir, "pbmc.h5")
file.exists(crb_output)
file.exists(h5_output)

crb <- readCerebro(crb_output)
crb$getExpressionBackend()
#> $type
#> [1] "h5"
#>
#> $location
#> [1] "pbmc.h5"

The on-disk matrix is stored as cells by genes in the /expression group, in the layout of HDF5Array::writeTENxMatrix(). CerebroNexus reconnects it lazily and exposes the usual genes-by-cells matrix to the application.

A thin .crb

The cell names are kept once, in the H5 file: /expression/genes holds the cell names and /expression/barcodes the gene names (the axis names follow the 10x convention for a genes-by-cells matrix, which is transposed here). The .crb itself is thin (schema version 5). It drops meta_data$cell_barcode and the row names of the projections, and instead stores a checksum of the cell names (cell_names_hash) together with the cell count. readCerebro() and the Viewer read the cell names back from the H5 file, verify the checksum and restore both fields, so the object you work with is identical to an embedded one:

head(crb$getMetaData()$cell_barcode)
rownames(crb$projections[[1]])[1:3]

If the .crb and the H5 file do not belong together, for example because the H5 file was re-exported with a different cell order, loading stops with an error instead of attaching expression values to the wrong cells (see Data integrity contracts).

Schema 5 uses a versioned XXH3-128 checksum (seed 0) of the ordered UTF-8 names, each terminated by a zero byte, independently of rlang and R-object serialization. Raw-byte encoding and hashing run in native code without temporary files. Existing schema-3/4 files require a one-time convertCerebro("dataset.crb") with the updated package; stop apps using the export first. Conversion validates the old checksum and reuses the H5 matrix without re-exporting expression. Rebuild its Viewer Pack if conversion did not already rebuild it. This applies to any thin H5 CRB, not just large datasets; embedded-expression CRBs are unaffected. Normal ordered-name validation still runs before expression access in each new Viewer process, without legacy-hash retries. Opening a schema-5 file requires an updated reader, including updated standalone apps.

Launch or bundle an H5-backed dataset

Keep the .crb and .h5 together and launch the .crb. Its descriptor tells CerebroNexus where to find the matrix, so no separate H5 argument is needed:

launchCerebro(
  crb_file_to_load = crb_output
)

For deployment, pass the .crb to createShinyApp(). It reads the same descriptor and copies the referenced H5 sidecar, and the immune repertoire sidecar if there is one, into the self-contained app bundle. The files are stored under the app’s private private-data/ tree and are not registered as browser-downloadable HTTP resources. There is no option to point the app at a different matrix path on the host: the .crb and its recorded sidecars are the only source.

createShinyApp(
  cerebro_data = c("PBMC" = crb_output),
  result_dir = file.path(output_dir, "pbmc_app"),
  launch_browser = FALSE
)

If the .crb is renamed, do not guess a new H5 name. The descriptor remains authoritative. Use crb$getExpressionBackend() to see the sidecar that belongs to the file.

Immune repertoire sidecar

A dataset with a very large immune repertoire gets a third file, <stem>.immune.qs2, next to the .crb and the .h5 file. By default (immune_sidecar = "auto" in exportFromSeurat() and saveCerebro()) this happens for H5-backed .crb files whose repertoire has at least immune_sidecar_threshold = 100000L rows; "always" and "never" override that decision. Move and bundle the sidecar together with the .crb like the H5 file.

Convert an existing embedded .crb

The direct export above is preferred for new Seurat exports. The manual workflow remains useful when only a current, embedded .crb is available, for example after an exportFromSCE() workflow, and the source object cannot be exported again.

Load the existing .crb, transpose its conventional genes-by-cells expression matrix, and write it to the /expression group:

crb_input <- system.file(
  "extdata/examples/example.crb",
  package = "CerebroNexus"
)
crb <- readCerebro(crb_input)

legacy_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "cerebro-legacy-h5")
dir.create(legacy_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
h5_output <- file.path(legacy_dir, "example.h5")

HDF5Array::writeTENxMatrix(
  Matrix::t(crb$expression),
  h5_output,
  group = "expression",
  level = 1L
)

Remove the embedded matrix and record the sibling filename before saving the smaller .crb; otherwise the original matrix will still be loaded into memory, or the saved object will not know where its external matrix lives. Because the backend is H5, saveCerebro() writes a thin .crb: it checks that the H5 cell names match meta_data$cell_barcode in the same order and then keeps only their checksum.

crb$expression <- NULL
crb$setExpressionBackend(
  type = "h5",
  location = basename(h5_output)
)
crb_output <- file.path(legacy_dir, "example.crb")
saveCerebro(crb, crb_output)

The converted .crb is now self-describing. Keep it beside example.h5 and launch it without any further argument:

launchCerebro(
  crb_file_to_load = crb_output
)

When the original Seurat object is available, exportFromSeurat(..., expression_matrix_mode = "h5") remains the preferred, less error-prone route.

Read, save and convert

This small example creates a portable CRB without downloading a dataset:

library(CerebroNexus)
cells <- c("cell-a", "cell-b", "cell-c")
object <- Cerebro$new()
object$setExpression(matrix(c(1, 0, 2, 3, 0, 4), nrow = 2,
  dimnames = list(c("gene-a", "gene-b"), cells)))
object$setMetaData(data.frame(cell_barcode = cells, sample = c("A", "A", "B")))
object$addProjection("umap", data.frame(x = 1:3, y = c(0, 1, 0), row.names = cells))
work <- tempfile("cerebro-guide-")
dir.create(work)
file <- file.path(work, "example.crb")
saveCerebro(object, file)
restored <- readCerebro(file)
stopifnot(identical(restored$getMetaData()$cell_barcode, cells))

readCerebro() reads RDS and qs2 CRBs; .crb describes the logical format, not its physical codec. saveCerebro(..., codec = "rds") requests RDS compatibility, while the default uses qs2. convertCerebro() re-serializes a CRB while reusing its existing expression data, so input and output must be in the same directory:

convertCerebro("study.crb", "study-rds.crb", codec = "rds")

convertCerebro() is also the one-time migration path for a CRB written by an older release; see Older files and retired formats.

Move the complete dataset

Keep paths recorded inside the CRB valid. A typical layout is:

study.crb
study.h5
study.immune.qs2   (only when the repertoire is large)
study.viewer/

Additional spatial molecule/image resources must also travel with their dataset. Do not rename or partially copy sidecars independently. RDS and qs2 versions of a CRB can share the same unchanged H5 file. The cell-order checksum stored in the .crb rejects an H5 file whose cells differ from the ones the .crb was written for.

For distribution, createShinyApp() builds a self-contained Viewer directory and copies the required resources. It resolves colliding CRB basenames and places each Viewer Pack beside the final CRB name. Follow the app creation guide.

Viewer Packs and fallback

Viewer Packs are optional derived assets for projection geometry, metadata and other prepared views. The CRB remains the source of truth. Build and validate a pack explicitly:

pack <- buildViewerPack(file, viewer_binary = "always")
stopifnot(validateViewerPack(file, pack)$valid)

Projection rows are aligned by barcode to canonical metadata order. Missing, duplicate or unmatched identities are rejected, even when row counts agree. Keep actual barcode row names on manually supplied projections.

After changing the CRB, rebuild with buildViewerPack(file, viewer_binary = "always", overwrite = TRUE). A missing, incompatible or stale pack, such as one written for another pack schema, is invalid as a whole and falls back to the ordinary data path; rebuilding it restores the fast paths.

A pack built before the Viewer stored the immune repertoire as integer columns (immune/encoded.qs2) is still valid, but its Immune repertoire page encodes the repertoire in memory at the first visit and says so: about 21 s on the 1.46 M-cell Ren data set, about 8 s on later starts (the encoding is kept in the user cache folder; CEREBRO_IR_CACHE changes it), against about 1 s with a current pack. Rebuild such a pack once with buildViewerPack("path/to/data.crb", overwrite = TRUE). Do not suppress checksum failures or edit a manifest to make a pack appear valid.

Understand large-group plots

Violin density uses at most 4,096 mid-quantile values per group on the original measurement scale. It is an approximation and can omit rare tails. Box quartiles, median, whiskers and mean are computed separately from all finite observations; hover also reports sample count, minimum and maximum. Missing/non-finite values are excluded. Approximate density is labelled in the summary hover. Display compaction never rescales observations to force an equal mean.

Launch the demos

The installed package includes small examples:

launchCerebro(crb_file_to_load = system.file(
  "extdata", "examples", "example.crb", package = "CerebroNexus"))

The complete large-data demo

The optional complete large-data launcher requires a repository checkout. Use a checkout of a published release tag for reproducible results, and record the printed commit ID when reporting them. The launcher loads that checkout directly.

git clone https://github.com/mihem/CerebroNexus.git
cd CerebroNexus
git rev-parse HEAD
Rscript -e "install.packages(c('remotes', 'pkgload')); remotes::install_local('.', dependencies = TRUE)"
Rscript run-demo.R

These demos keep their expression matrices in H5 sidecars and need no extra package beyond the ones CerebroNexus installs.

Open http://127.0.0.1:7451. The first run downloads and prepares the official 10x one-million-neuron matrix and the Ren et al. COVID-19 immune atlas (GEO GSE158055; 1,462,702 cells, all 64 published cell populations, sample/patient clinical metadata, and 220,968 paired-TCR plus 282,464 paired-BCR cells). The initial compressed downloads total about 18 GB. The prepared H5 files are written uncompressed and take considerable disk space on top of the extracted matrices, so allow a generous amount of free cache space. Source and prepared files are cached outside the repository (set CEREBRO_LARGE_CACHE to choose the location), so later runs reuse them.

To test Ren without the 10x dataset, and to separate download/preparation failures from Viewer errors (--prepare-only exits before starting Shiny):

Rscript run-demo.R --data=ren --prepare-only
Rscript run-demo.R --data=ren

The launcher prints the URL, the source directory and the Ren data version (currently 2), and reuses a complete compatible cache. Keep each .crb and its .h5 file together. Prepared versions use separate directories (ren/cerebro-v2/); preparation never upgrades the earlier ren/cerebro/ atlas in place, failed builds are not published, and source downloads are shared between versions.

The launcher also builds each data set’s Viewer Pack and rebuilds it when it is missing or predates an asset the viewer reads (the HLA first frames, the immune repertoire’s integer encoding). Without a pack, the HLA & TCR motifs page spends about 15 s (about 25 s for the whole first entry) building the CDR3 Hamming-1 graph at Ren’s scale; with one, the same entry settles in under two seconds. If you start the viewer against a prepared .crb yourself, build the pack once (about a minute for Ren) with buildViewerPack("path/to/data.crb", overwrite = TRUE); rerunning it after re-preparing a CRB is also the repair.

The 10x marker-guided E18 neurogenesis path excludes endothelial, microglial and oligodendrocyte programs, orders the remaining neural lineage with early, transitional and late markers, and separates excitatory and inhibitory terminal branches. It is a labelled demonstration, not a formal trajectory-inference result. The same app also includes the bundled PBMC, immune-repertoire, trajectory, spatial, Trekker and HLA/TCR demos. See the benchmark guide before starting.

Older files and retired formats

Only the current layout is read. readCerebro(), launchCerebro(), createShinyApp() and the Viewer reject an older .crb, for example one that has no expression-backend descriptor, uses a thin schema other than version 5, or still stores receptors in the bcr_data / tcr_data fields, with

The Cerebro data file 'x.crb' uses a retired format: <reason>.
Convert it once with CerebroNexus::convertCerebro().

convertCerebro() is the only migration path. It sets a missing descriptor to embedded, merges the old receptor fields into the unified immune repertoire, updates the ordered-name checksum of schema-3/4 files to portable schema 5, and rewrites an H5-backed .crb from CerebroNexus 5.1.x (which carried its cell names in the .crb) as a thin one next to its existing H5 file:

convertCerebro("old_dataset.crb")

A .crb whose expression storage this version cannot read or repair (an expression backend other than embedded or h5, thin schema 1 or 2, or an immune sidecar of another type than "file") is rejected and cannot be converted. Re-export it from the source Seurat object with exportFromSeurat(..., expression_matrix_mode = "h5").

Viewer options for large data

Set these with options() before launchCerebro(), or in the .Rprofile of a server that hosts the Viewer.

Option Default What it does
cerebro.crb_cache_slots 2 How many loaded .crb files the R process keeps, so a later session or a switch back to a data set does not read the file again. Each one keeps its metadata and projections in memory.
cerebro.idle_initial_delay 1.2 Seconds a new session must be quiet (no click, no frame asked for) before the Viewer prepares the pages that are not open yet.
cerebro.idle_delay 2 The same after any later activity. Values below 0.05 fall back to the default.
cerebro.dev_reload FALSE For work on the Viewer itself: TRUE checks the installed Viewer source files for changes in every session. Otherwise an installed package’s files are read once per process.

Sessions on the same data set file also share what they compute (the sorted gene list, ROI scopes, the trajectory’s cells, clonal UMAP points). Each kind keeps a few entries, and all are dropped when the last session ends.

Troubleshooting

  • Missing sidecar: restore the recorded sibling .h5 (or .immune.qs2) file. A thin CRB alone is not a complete external dataset.
  • Retired format: convert the file once with convertCerebro(), or re-export a dataset whose storage this version cannot read from its source Seurat object.
  • Identity/checksum mismatch: restore the matching sidecar or re-export from a consistent source. Equal cell counts do not prove correct cell correspondence.
  • Pack rejected or slower fallback: rebuild the optional pack from the current CRB; preserve the CRB and expression data.
  • Memory pressure: inspect matrix density and format; avoid dense realization. A disk backend does not make every upstream Seurat operation out-of-core.
  • Slow first operation: distinguish package loading, backend reads and browser painting. A warm revisit is not a cold-start measurement.
